extracted.intended_audience: paediatricians, clinician-researchers, journal editors, and others interested in the history and practice of academic peer review
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive overview of the historical evolution, models, and current challenges of scholarly peer review intended to inform readers about how peer review developed and what criteria and tensions shape its practice today.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of peer review (editorial selection and quality control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing (later called ‘peer review’) began as a simple tool to help journal editors select papers and gradually developed into the rigorous quality-control system in scholarly publishing today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally used to help editors choose which papers to publish; decisions were often influenced by personal preferences. Over time the purpose expanded to include subject-matter expertise and quality control, aiming to ensure high-quality papers with minimal errors (as exemplified by Ernest Hart at BMJ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external subject-matter expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sent manuscripts to subject matter experts to determine whether they should be selected for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inviting external experts became common practice in learned societies (e.g., Royal Society practices). The rationale was increasing complexity and specialization in research requiring expert knowledge. This remains a core criterion for evaluating review rigor: do reviewers have appropriate expertise?

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial committees and collective decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Formation of committees (e.g., a 'Committee on Papers') that invited external experts and collectively advised on publication decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee review structures historically formalized editorial oversight; such structures aim to support consistent selection but can produce conflicting reports (a challenge noted since Whewell’s time). Assessment of a review system should consider whether editorial decision-making processes are structured and transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written reviewer reports and transparency (publishing reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal that reviewers provide written evaluations and that these reports could be published to encourage submissions and widen dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whewell suggested publishing reviewers’ reports in Proceedings of the Royal Society to increase transparency and encourage submissions. Modern assessments consider whether review reports are documented, shared with authors, or publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized editorial workflow (suitability check then peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern standardized process: the editor-in-chief checks manuscript suitability and scope fit, then sends it for peer review; reviewers submit feedback including a recommended final decision, enabling editors to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This workflow is now the norm in many journals and is a baseline criterion for a functioning peer-review system — clarity of roles, initial screening, and structured reviewer recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding systems (single-blind and double-blind review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Growing concerns about demographic and reputational biases led journals to adopt single-blind and double-blind review systems to promote fairer reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blinding is intended to reduce bias based on author identity or reputation; effectiveness is debated and may have declined in the digital age. Evaluation should consider which blinding model is used and evidence about its impact on fairness and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint model (early online sharing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints were introduced as a response to perceptions that peer review was time-consuming, biased and inconsistent, allowing online sharing of minimally screened papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints accelerate dissemination and are central to open science debates; assessing a publication ecosystem involves weighing speed and openness against lack of formal peer review prior to public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication review (launched by F1000) publishes papers after a basic in-house check, with evaluation occurring openly after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model shifts formal evaluation to after publication, aiming for rapid dissemination and community evaluation. When evaluating systems, consider whether post-publication review includes adequate checks and whether open community critique is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review (identity disclosure and transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review reveals the identities of reviewer and author and aims for constructive feedback, formal recognition of reviewers, more transparency and less bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ pioneered open peer review; the term now covers several models. Advantages cited include constructive feedback for authors, reviewer recognition, reduced bias, and guidance for early-career reviewers. Evaluation should consider which open-peer features are adopted and their effects on fairness, recognition, and feedback quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization of journal publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercialization of society publication: societies relying on major publishers to manage cost and scale, affecting journal production and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As publication scaled, many societies outsourced to commercial publishers. This structural change influences peer review workflows, incentives, and scalability; assessments should consider publisher policies and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer acknowledgement and formal recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Growing interest in formally recognizing reviewer contribution (e.g., Publons, ORCID integration, reviewer certificates and awards), addressing concerns that peer review is under-recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition mechanisms aim to incentivize quality reviewing and integrate review activity into researcher profiles. Evaluation of a system can include whether reviewer contributions are tracked, credited, or rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer fatigue and availability of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer fatigue: increasing submission volumes are disproportionate to available reviewers, leading to overwork and low-quality feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key measure of peer-review health is reviewer supply and workload; chronic overload can degrade review quality. Consider reviewer recruitment, workload distribution, and support mechanisms when assessing systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed, timeliness, and cost of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with digital processes, peer review is slow, time-consuming (especially to find reviewers), and expensive, leading to delays in publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed affects researcher careers and the timeliness of findings. Evaluation should balance speed with thoroughness, considering turnaround times, editorial triage, and resources used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness at detecting research misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges in detecting misconduct: growing concern that peer review isn’t equipped to detect research misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review was not primarily designed to detect fraud; assessment should consider complementary mechanisms (e.g., data checks, reproducibility reviews, editorial screening) and whether the review process includes safeguards against misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption and cultural norms across regions/fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical variation in adoption: peer review became central in some regions/fields earlier than others (e.g., uptake in UK/North America; later global spread influenced by American funding agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of peer-review practices should account for disciplinary and regional norms, recognizing that expectations and standards vary internationally and by field.
